processing: Revived products include a black tea and drinks named for 河越 matcha and hojicha; as a green tea it follows the steamed method usual in the Sayama area.
harvest_season: As in neighbouring Sayama, there are typically two pickings: first flush shipped in April to May, second in June to July.
appearance_dry: Typically deep green needles, as with Sayama sencha.
appearance_liquor: Typically yellow-green and clear, as with Sayama sencha.
appearance_wet: Typically soft green leaf, as with Sayama sencha.
taste_profile: Little is documented about its own taste; expect something in the family of Sayama steamed greens, with a fresh and fairly full character.

brewing.notes: Standard starting point for a Japanese steamed green; adjust by taste.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's crop as usual for Japanese greens, with the first flush most valued. The revived name also appears on black tea and on matcha and hojicha drinks, so read the label for what you are actually buying.
description:
Kawagoe-cha is an old name for tea from the former Kawagoe domain in Saitama, recently brought back. Today's Kawagoe tea is grown in areas including Kawagoe, Sayama and Tokorozawa, so think of it as a branch of the Sayama tea world under a historic label.

The spelling shifts: older usage writes it 河越茶, and modern labels may use either that or 川越茶. It covers more than one product, including a black tea, 小江戸和紅茶, and milk drinks named for 河越 matcha and hojicha.

Little is documented about how it differs in the cup from other Sayama tea. Brew a green one as you would a sencha and compare it side by side with a labelled Sayama-cha.

Saitama also has two other place-labelled teas, Chichibu and Kodama, so look for a stated garden or maker rather than relying on the name alone.
history:
The Kawagoe area was already reputed for tea in the 14th century, when one account calls it a leading tea region of the realm. In the Edo period, many villages of the Sayama hills belonged to the Kawagoe domain, and their tea went by the name 河越茶. Land development in the mid-Edo period spread cultivation further.

The name later dropped out of everyday use in favour of Sayama tea. One local article says it was revived a little over ten years before its writing.
